{{short description|American biologist}}
'''Melissa Suzanne Cline''' is an American biologist. She is an Associate Research Scientist at the [[UC Santa Cruz Genomics Institute]]
Between June 2001 and December 2004 she was a staff scientist at Affymetrix, Inc. in [[Emeryville, California]] where she was involved in developing ANOSVA, a "statistical method to identify alternative spicing from expression data," during which she "analyzed the effects of alternative splicing on protein [[transmembrane]] and signal [[peptide]] regions".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://users.soe.ucsc.edu/~cline/cline.pdf|title=Melissa Susanne Cline|publisher=University of California, Santa Cruz|accessdate=14 November 2015}}</ref>  Subsequently, she moved to UC Santa Cruz, where she wrote on genome browsing.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cline |first1=Melissa S |last2=Kent |first2=W James |date=2009-02-01 |title=Understanding genome browsing |url=http://www.nature.com/articles/nbt0209-153 |journal=Nature Biotechnology |language=en |volume=27 |issue=2 |pages=153–155 |doi=10.1038/nbt0209-153 |pmid=19204697 |s2cid=205265560 |issn=1087-0156|url-access=subscription }}</ref> According to the Thomson [[Reuters]] report, she was one of the most highly cited scientists in the world in 2012/13.<ref name="Highly cited">{{cite web|title=The World's Most Influential Scientific Minds 2014|url=http://sites.biology.duke.edu/donglab/images/papers/thomas_reuter_2014.pdf|publisher=Thomson Reuters|accessdate=14 November 2015|location=Duke University, Durham, North Carolina|date=2014|page=13|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20151117020628/http://sites.biology.duke.edu/donglab/images/papers/thomas_reuter_2014.pdf|archivedate=17 November 2015}}</ref> 

Cline is currently the program manager for the [https://brcaexchange.org BRCA Exchange], a platform that shares knowledge on the tens of thousands of [[BRCA1|''BRCA 1'']] and [[BRCA2|''BRCA 2'']] genetic variants that could influence a person's susceptibility to breast cancer, particularly on the clinical significance of those variants.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Miyatsu |first=Rose |date=October 23, 2023 |title=Working to improve clarity for patients assessing their genetic breast cancer risk |url=https://news.ucsc.edu/2023/10/brca-exchange-23.html }}</ref>   One of the challenge in curating the clinical impact of genetic variants is that is the curation often relies on clinical evidence of the variants in patients and their families; to protect patient privacy, most genetic data is ''siloed'', or maintained in closed databases where the data are inaccessible to most researchers.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Diamond |first=Joel |date=July 13, 2018 |title=Don't lock genomic data into silos |work=MedCity News |url=https://medcitynews.com/2018/07/de-siloing-genomic-data/}}</ref>  Addressing this problem, Dr. Cline and colleagues devised a "federated analysis" approach to analyze patient data within its secure home repository, gathering new knowledge for variant curation while safeguarding patient privacy.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cline |first=Melissa |date=August 2023 |title=Federated Analysis for Privacy-Preserving Data Sharing: A Technical and Legal Primer |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/full/10.1146/annurev-genom-110122-084756 |journal=Annual Review of Genomics and Human Genetics |volume=24 |pages=347–368|doi=10.1146/annurev-genom-110122-084756 |doi-access=free |pmc=10846631 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cline |first=Melissa |date=March 9, 2022 |title=Federated analysis of BRCA1 and BRCA2 variation in a Japanese cohort |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2666979X22000295 |journal=Cell Genomics |volume=2 |issue=3}}</ref>  This approach has successfully gathered new variant knowledge from siloed data, advancing the curation of ''BRCA'' variants.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 3, 2022 |title=How a bot beamed from California to Japan may stop unnecessary mastectomies for breast cancer patients |url=https://www.ga4gh.org/news_item/how-a-bot-beamed-from-california-to-japan-may-prevent-cancer-patients-from-losing-their-breasts-unnecessarily/ |website=Global Alliance for Genomics and Health News}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Borfitz |first=Deborah |date=June 14, 2022 |title='Federated Analysis' Helps Fill Genetic Risk Knowledge Gap On BRCA Genes |work=Bio-IT World |url=https://www.bio-itworld.com/news/2022/06/14/federated-analysis-helps-fill-genetic-risk-knowledge-gap-on-brca-genes }}</ref>
